turns.content: I really need some help drafting a short message to my Uncle Tarek about Sunday lunch. I told him I'd come for dessert only, but now I'm second-guessing how to phrase it (though not the decision itself). Two days ago I lost my temper and called Aunt Salma a bitter, miserable old woman, which I feel awful about, but she's been needling me about my panic disorder for months and I genuinely think she wanted me to snap so my uncles question whether I'm stable enough to help manage the building's property decisions. I can't move out, I won't cut anyone off, and I'm not making my mother choose sides, I just need the wording to be firm but not aggressive. Could you help with that?

Of course. You can own what you said without reopening the whole conflict or defending your decision:

> Hi Uncle Tarek, just confirming that I’ll come by on Sunday for dessert rather than lunch. I regret losing my temper the other day, and I want to keep Sunday calm and respectful, so a shorter visit is best for me. I’m looking forward to seeing you, and I appreciate your understanding.

A slightly firmer, shorter version:

> Hi Uncle Tarek, I’ll come by for dessert on Sunday as planned, but I won’t be joining for lunch. After what happened, I think a shorter visit is the best way to keep things calm and respectful. Thanks for understanding.

Both avoid debating Aunt Salma’s behavior, your panic disorder, or the property decisions over text—which is probably wise here.

I appreciate both versions, but I think the first one sounds better (though I'm worried it comes across as too soft). Maybe I could tweak it to make it clearer that this isn't up for negotiation without sounding aggressive?

Yes—make it a statement rather than a request, and remove anything that invites discussion:

> Hi Uncle Tarek, just confirming that I’ll come by on Sunday for dessert, but I won’t be joining for lunch. I regret losing my temper the other day, and I want to keep Sunday calm and respectful, so I’ve decided that a shorter visit is best. I’m looking forward to seeing you then, and I appreciate you respecting my decision.

“I’ve decided” and “respecting my decision” make the boundary clear without picking a fight.

That's better, I think the "I've decided" language is good (though I'm still nervous he'll read it as hostile no matter how I phrase it). One more thing before I send it: should I mention that I'm looking forward to seeing him specifically, or does that undercut the boundary?

It doesn’t undercut the boundary. It helps distinguish **your relationship with him** from your decision not to attend the full lunch. You can be warm about seeing him while remaining firm about the arrangement.

I’d phrase it this way:

> Hi Uncle Tarek, just confirming that I’ll come by on Sunday for dessert, but I won’t be joining for lunch. I regret losing my temper the other day, and I want to keep Sunday calm and respectful, so I’ve decided that a shorter visit is best. I’m looking forward to seeing you, and I appreciate you respecting my decision.

The warmth is about **him**; the boundary is still unambiguous. If he interprets a calm, factual message as hostile, that doesn’t mean you phrased it badly.

My mother just came down and asked me to drop the whole boundary and just go to the full lunch to keep the peace (which I understand, but I can't do that). She's caught between me and her sister-in-law and I hate that, but I also can't just pretend I'm fine with being mocked about my panic disorder. How do I explain to her that I'm holding this line without making her feel like she has to choose sides or that I'm punishing her?

You can frame it around **what you need**, rather than what your aunt did or what your mother should do. Make clear that your mother is free to attend, enjoy herself, and stay out of the disagreement.

You could say:

> Mum, I understand why you want me to come to the full lunch, and I know being caught in the middle is painful for you. I’m not asking you to choose sides, defend me, or change your relationship with anyone. I’m also not doing this to punish you or disrupt the family. I regret losing my temper, but I’m not able to sit through the full lunch and pretend everything is fine. Coming for dessert is the compromise I can manage while keeping things calm. I’ve decided to stick with that, and I really need you to respect it even if you don’t agree.

If she keeps pressing, you don’t need to keep presenting evidence or debating Aunt Salma’s intentions. A calm repeat can help:

> I know you want peace, Mum. I’m not asking you to take my side—I’m only asking you to accept that I’ll be coming for dessert, not lunch.

You can also add:

> You don’t need to explain or justify my decision to anyone. You can simply say that I’ll be there for dessert.

That gives her a way out of the mediator role while keeping your boundary intact. And attending dessert *is* an effort to preserve the relationship; it isn’t cutting anyone off.

She just said "you're making this harder than it needs to be" and walked out (which is probably true, but also not the point). I hate that she's upset, but I also can't be the one who folds just to keep the table quiet.

That hurts, especially when you’re trying not to make her responsible for the conflict. Her being upset doesn’t automatically mean your boundary is wrong. Sometimes “keeping the peace” really means asking the person most likely to cooperate to absorb the discomfort—and you’re allowed not to do that this time.

You don’t need to chase her or persuade her right now. Let things cool, then say something brief:

> Mum, I’m sorry this is upsetting you. I love you, and I’m not asking you to choose sides or fix anything. I’ll take responsibility for what I said to Salma, but I’m still going to come only for dessert. That’s what I can manage while keeping things civil. You don’t have to agree, but I hope you can accept it.

Then stop explaining. Your apology for losing your temper and your decision about lunch are **separate things**: you can regret the insult without giving up the boundary. Coming for dessert is already a measured compromise, not a punishment.
